front: most common site for an ectopic pregnancy

front: some primary risk factors for ectopic pregnancy

inflammation resulting in tubal damage (salpingitis, acute chlamydial infection or even the presence of chlamydial antigens)
pregnancy after tubal sterilization
prior ectopic pregnancy 
prior tubal surgery
endocrine factors (t1dm)

front: the classic symptoms of ectopic pregnancy
back:
amenorrhea followed by vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain on the affected side
can also have some bleeding or decidual cast

in normal pregnancy, b hcg levels rise in a log-linear way until about 60-80d after the last menses, levels then plateau at 100,000

anything less than this sus for an ectopic

front: at what hCG level can TVS detect an intauterine gestation?

front: some primary etiologic factors of spontaneous abortion

infectious: chlamydia, listeria, HIV, GBS colonization

enviro: cigarette smoking, alcohol, large amount of rads exposure
uterine: large and multiple uterine leiomyomas or Asherman syndrome

front: threatened abortion
back:

usually poor prognosis indicated by persistent bleeding and pain

front: inevitable abortion
back:
vaginal bleeding or gross rupture of the membranes in the presence of cervical dilation, followed by uterine contractions
should not attempt to prolong pregnancy

front: incomplete vs complete abortion

incomplete: internal cervical os opens and allows the passage of blood and some tissue; some tissue is retained and needs to be extracted 
complete: documented pregnancy that spontaneously passes all contents of the uterus

front: missed abortion
back: retention of a failed intrauterine pregnancy for an extended period, mostly no symptoms and will proceed to expul spontaneously

front: options for first-trimester medical abortion

front: options for second-trimester abortion

medical is uncommon after 70d gestation
